hints: Focus on the last two steps, where a white precipitate forms and then disappears in excess NaOH. Which type of hydroxide behaves like that?
Recall that aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric and redissolves to give $\text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^-$, while $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ and $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ stay as precipitates.
Check the start of the sequence too: the metal must burn to give a white oxide that dissolves in dilute HCl to make a chloride solution ready for that precipitate test.
walkthrough:
**Read the key clue at the end**

The most telling part is white precipitate to solution in excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$. That is the classic test for an amphoteric hydroxide.

$$\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^-(aq)$$

**Work backwards through the middle**

Before that, we had a solution plus $\text{NaOH}$ giving that white precipitate. This fits $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ions forming $\text{Al(OH)}_3$.

$$\text{Al}^{3+}(aq) + 3\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3(s)$$

**Check the start with burning in oxygen**

Aluminium burns to form a white solid oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, which is basic enough to react with dilute $\text{HCl}$ to give a solution of $\text{AlCl}_3$.

$$4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$

**Put the whole chain together**

Only aluminium gives white oxide, then $\text{Al}^{3+}$ solution, then white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate, then clear aluminate solution in excess alkali. This matches every arrow perfectly.

options.A: Aluminium fits all steps. It burns to white $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, which dissolves in $\text{HCl}$ to $\text{AlCl}_3$ solution. Adding $\text{NaOH}$ gives white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ precipitate, which is amphoteric and dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to form colourless $\text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^-$ solution.
options.B: Calcium burns to white $\text{CaO}$ and forms $\text{CaCl}_2$ solution, and $\text{NaOH}$ can give a white $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ precipitate. However $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is basic, not amphoteric, so it does not dissolve in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to give a solution.
options.C: Magnesium burns to white $\text{MgO}$ and forms $\text{MgCl}_2$ solution, and $\text{NaOH}$ gives white $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ precipitate. The trap is stopping there, but $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is basic only and is insoluble in excess $\text{NaOH}$, so the final solution would not form.
options.D: Phosphorus burns to a white solid $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, but this is an acidic oxide. It would dissolve in water or alkali directly to give phosphate solution, not form a chloride solution that then gives a white precipitate with $\text{NaOH}$ that redissolves.
